Bitcoin transactions.
By way of comparison, according to information reported publicly, in 2012 Western
Union made remittances totaling approximately $81 billion, PayPal processed approximately

trillion in transactions, and Bank of America processed $244.4 trillion in wire transfers.
This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was
$1.6 trillion.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: No. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) imposes suspicious activity reporting duties on financial institutions, and the facts only describe an individual’s transactions without identifying any covered financial institution’s SAR obligation or failure to report.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates that the Secretary require a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation” (i.e., SAR filing requirements), and provides related protections (e.g., safe harbor and confidentiality) tied to such reporting. Here, the fact pattern describes Entity SYN_908f79e2 as an individual in US-CA with various card/ACH/wire/cash transactions and an expected monthly volume, but it does not identify (1) any specific “financial institution” subject to § 5318(g) requirements, (2) whether any transaction was deemed “suspicious” under applicable implementing rules, or (3) whether a SAR was required, filed, or not filed. Because the statute’s operative duties attach to a financial institution’s reporting, and the facts only show an individual’s activity without the necessary institutional reporting context, applicability cannot be determined. Contiguous phrase in answer: “31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) imposes suspicious”.
